## Learning Objectives {.compact}

By the end of this week, you should be able to:

1. Choose an epidemiologic data source that fits a research question.
2. Match a mortality numerator to an appropriate population denominator.
3. Explain how coverage, classification, and reporting affect our conclusions.
4. Distinguish vital statistics, case reporting, surveys, and syndromic surveillance.
5. Explain how international coordination improves disease monitoring.

::: {.notes}
Recall a measure from the previous module. Today we ask where its numerator and denominator come from, and what they allow us to conclude.

Allow about 90 minutes across class meetings for the core deck, including 12–15 minutes for the opening quiz and transitions. A natural stopping point is after the Census exercise. Allow a further 9 minutes for the optional Google Trends extension. Shorten voluntary reports if discussion runs long; preserve the final checks on learning.

Students work in pairs or existing project groups with one browser and calculator per group. Written scenarios work on paper; the retrieval exercises include displayable data fallbacks. Invite volunteers to share without asking students to disclose personal health experiences.
:::

## Primary and Secondary Data

**Primary collection:** Gather new observations for our question.

**Secondary use:** Analyze data that already exist.

Either can help us understand health—even when the records contain no diagnoses.

::: {.notes}
Allow 1 minute. A survey we design is primary collection; reusing an existing survey, medical records, or Census estimates is secondary use. The same dataset can be primary for its original investigators and secondary for another analysis. Neither label guarantees quality.
:::

## Exercise: Primary vs. Secondary Data

**Fictional scenario · Pairs · 5 minutes**

Our county wants to understand barriers to staying safe during extreme heat. We can fund one initial approach:

**A.** Interview residents about cooling access and transportation.

**B.** Analyze existing emergency-department records of heat illness.

**C.** Combine existing housing, tree-cover, and population data.

Which would we start with? Give one reason and one question it would leave unanswered.

::: {.notes}
Allow 1 minute to choose, 2 to discuss, and 2 to compare reasoning. A directly measures experiences but requires recruitment. B captures serious illness and healthcare use, missing people who do not reach an ED. C helps identify environmental conditions but cannot identify who became ill. Clarify that B and C are secondary uses; A collects new data. No single correct choice without a more precise question. Fallback: write a letter and reason on paper, then invite voluntary reports.
:::

## Vital Statistics

Birth and death records describe events in a population.

State and local registration systems supply data to the **National Vital Statistics System (NVSS)** at CDC’s National Center for Health Statistics.

A death can be registered even when its cause is classified incorrectly.

::: {.notes}
Allow 1 minute. Vital events also include fetal deaths, marriages, and divorces; today's examples focus on mortality. NVSS provides national birth, death, and fetal-death statistics. Avoid equating broad registration coverage with error-free or instantly available records. Source: [CDC NVSS](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nvss/index.htm).
:::

## Exercise: Vital-Statistics Retrieval

**Pairs · 8 minutes**

Open [CDC’s *Mortality in the United States, 2024*](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/products/databriefs/db548.htm). Each pair takes one task:

- **A. Life expectancy:** Find life expectancy at birth. Explain why it is not a promise about how long a particular newborn will live.

- **B. Death rates:** Find the age-adjusted death rates for 2023 and 2024. Explain what age adjustment contributes to the comparison.

- **C. Leading causes:** Find which cause entered the top ten in 2024. Did its age-adjusted death rate increase?

Produce two sentences: one accurate finding with year and units, and one interpretation or limitation.

::: {.notes}
- **How to run it and timing:** **8 minutes:** 1 minute to assign tasks, 3 for retrieval, 1 to write, and 3 for up to three voluntary reports and synthesis. If the website is unavailable, use the data on the next slide; ask students to interpret the supplied values.
- **Instructor notes and debrief:**  Verified answers are **79.0 years**; **750.5 versus 722.1 deaths per 100,000 standard population**; and **suicide**, whose age-adjusted rate declined from **14.1 to 13.7** even as it became the tenth leading cause. [CDC brief](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/products/databriefs/db548.htm).
- Life expectancy summarizes mortality conditions; age adjustment facilitates comparisons accounting for age composition. Ranking is relative to other causes, so a rank can rise while a rate falls. Ask: “Which finding would we use to compare mortality across populations with different age structures?”
- **Takeaway:** Report the measure and its meaning together.
:::


## Mortality Data for the Exercise {.compact}

[CDC: Mortality in the United States, 2024](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/products/databriefs/db548.htm)

| Measure | 2023 | 2024 |
|---|---:|---:|
| Life expectancy at birth | 78.4 years | 79.0 years |
| All-cause age-adjusted death rate | 750.5 | 722.1 |
| Suicide age-adjusted death rate | 14.1 | 13.7 |

Rates are deaths per 100,000 U.S. standard population.

Suicide entered the ten leading causes in 2024; COVID-19 dropped out.

::: {.notes}
Use as a debrief after retrieval, or display throughout if internet access fails. Values come from CDC Data Brief 548, January 2026, tables 1, 2, and 4. Life expectancy applies the period's age-specific mortality conditions; it does not predict one child's lifespan. Age adjustment supports comparisons with a common age distribution. Keep this debrief within the preceding exercise's 8 minutes.
:::

## Exercise: Rank and Rate

**Pairs · 3 minutes**

Suicide entered the ten leading causes of death in 2024, while its age-adjusted death rate fell from **14.1 to 13.7 per 100,000**.

A headline says: “Suicide became a leading cause because the death rate increased.”

How would we correct the headline?

What does rank tell us that a population death rate does not?

::: {.notes}
Allow 1 minute to write and 2 to debrief. Ranking compares causes by their numbers of deaths. A cause's rank can rise when deaths from another cause decline more. A population death rate uses a population denominator; proportionate mortality uses all deaths as its denominator. Neither rank nor proportionate mortality is an individual's risk. Age-adjusted rates are comparative summary measures, not individual probabilities. Fallback: write the correction on paper. Source: [CDC Data Brief 548](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/products/databriefs/db548.htm), tables 2 and 4.
:::

## Exercise: One Death, Several Conditions

**Fictional teaching case · Pairs · 8 minutes**

The certifying clinician documents this sequence:

COVID-19 → pneumonia → acute respiratory distress syndrome → death.

The clinician also documents diabetes as contributing to the death.

A reader says: “The person died of respiratory distress, so this should not count as a COVID-19 death.”

In two sentences, explain what the reader has misunderstood. Then identify one uncertainty that could still affect the accuracy of the death certificate.

::: {.notes}
**How to run it and timing:** **8 minutes:** 1 minute to explain the documented sequence, 2 for individual writing, 2 for pairs, and 3 for debrief. Introduce “underlying” as the condition initiating the sequence; students need not diagnose the case.

**Instructor notes and debrief:** In this supplied sequence, COVID-19 is the underlying cause, respiratory distress syndrome the immediate cause, and diabetes an additional contributing condition. Multiple listed conditions do not negate the underlying cause. CDC’s certification guidance explicitly illustrates reporting COVID-19 together with pneumonia and respiratory distress. [CDC guidance](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/86558)

Legitimate uncertainties include incomplete clinical information and errors in documenting the sequence. A listed sequence can still be wrong. Fallback: use the written case and collect responses on paper.

Ask: “How would ‘deaths with COVID-19 listed anywhere’ differ from ‘deaths with COVID-19 as the underlying cause’?”

**Takeaway:** Complete death registration and accurate cause classification are different qualities.
:::


## Exercise: The Population Denominator

**Pairs · 9 minutes**

**Simulated numerator:** During 2025, 2,248 Tarrant County residents died from a fictional condition.

Open [Census QuickFacts: Tarrant County](https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/tarrantcountytexas).

1. Find the population estimate most appropriate for this numerator. Record its value and date.

2. Calculate deaths per 100,000 residents.

3. Explain why the 2020 Census count is less suitable.

**Extension:** If the deaths were only among residents aged 65 or older, what would need to change?

::: {.notes}
**How to run it and timing:** **9 minutes:** 1 minute of instructions, 3 for retrieval, 2 for calculation, and 3 for comparison and the extension. Pairs need a browser and calculator. If the website is unavailable, use the two population figures on the next slide.

**Instructor notes and debrief:** QuickFacts, checked September 11, 2026, reports **2,248,466 residents on July 1, 2025**, and a **2020 Census count of 2,110,640**. [Census source](https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/tarrantcountytexas)

The intended calculation is:

$$
\frac{2,248}{2,248,466} \times 100,000 \approx 100.0
$$

Using the 2020 count gives **106.5 per 100,000**. The difference arises entirely from denominator selection. For deaths among older residents, use the corresponding older population, with compatible geography and year.

Ask: “Would the same denominator work for deaths occurring in Tarrant County hospitals, including nonresidents?”

**Takeaway:** A plausible population number is not necessarily the correct denominator.
:::





## Population Data for the Exercise

[Census QuickFacts: Tarrant County, Texas](https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/tarrantcountytexas)

| Population measure | Residents |
|---|---:|
| July 1, 2025 population estimate | 2,248,466 |
| April 1, 2020 Census count | 2,110,640 |

Our simulated numerator is **2,248 resident deaths in 2025**.

Which denominator fits? Calculate deaths per 100,000 residents.

::: {.notes}
Display after retrieval, or use during the exercise if offline. These are Census values checked September 11, 2026; the deaths are fictional. The 2025 midyear estimate approximates the population exposed over that calendar year. Do not confuse the 2020 Census count with the separate estimates-base row. Expected results: 99.98 (about 100.0), versus 106.51 (about 106.5) using the older count. Pause here if splitting the module across meetings.
:::

## The DETECT Story

Medics can observe older adults in their homes during emergency calls.

DETECT introduced structured screening into that work. In the pilot, medic reports of suspected elder abuse to Adult Protective Services increased.

Does an increase in reports mean an increase in mistreatment?

::: {.notes}
Use 1 minute of the next exercise's 8-minute allocation for the story. Explain that routine EMS and APS records were created to deliver services and document responses. They can also help answer research questions. The pilot involved MedStar medics and community-dwelling patients aged 65 or older. Its finding concerns reports, not proof that underlying occurrence increased. [Cannell et al., DETECT pilot](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30614399/). The following numbers are a separate simulation, not results from this paper.
:::

## Exercise: Reports Doubled

**Simulated data—not DETECT results · Pairs · 8 minutes with story**

| Equal-length period | Eligible EMS encounters | Encounters generating a report |
|---|---:|---:|
| Before structured screening | 1,000 | 20 |
| After structured screening | 1,000 | 40 |

A draft headline says: “Elder mistreatment doubled.”

Write a more defensible headline. Name one additional piece of evidence that would help distinguish increased detection from increased occurrence.

::: {.notes}
After the story: 3 minutes to calculate and rewrite, 1 to submit, and 3 to discuss. Reporting rose from 2% to 4% of eligible encounters: a 2-percentage-point increase and a doubling. A defensible headline: “The percentage of eligible EMS encounters generating a report doubled after screening began.”

Better recognition, different reporting practices, changed patient mix, and changed occurrence could all contribute. Useful evidence includes comparable measures collected independently of screening, patient characteristics, and screening completion. A report records suspicion; it does not confirm mistreatment. Encounters need not represent unique people. Fallback: use the displayed table and unsigned paper responses.
:::

## Data Quality Questions

**Coverage:** Who never entered the records?

**Accuracy:** Was the event classified correctly?

**Consistency:** Did definitions or collection practices change?

**Timeliness:** Are records recent enough for the decision?

**Processing:** Were records duplicated, lost, or miscoded?

::: {.notes}
Allow 2 minutes. Ask pairs to connect one question to an earlier example: EMS access, death-certificate classification, DETECT screening, delayed reports, or duplicate encounters. A large database does not automatically solve these problems. Fallback: give a spoken example or write one sentence.
:::

## Exercise: A Case Reaches Public Health

**Fictional scenario · Pairs · 5 minutes**

A laboratory identifies a condition that must be reported under its state’s rules.

Put these steps in order:

- CDC combines case notifications for national monitoring.
- The laboratory reports to the appropriate health department.
- The health department investigates and applies the surveillance case definition.

Where could a person with the same disease be missed entirely?

::: {.notes}
Allow 2 minutes to order and identify a gap, then 3 to discuss with the next slide. Correct sequence: laboratory report, health-department investigation/classification, national notification. Some people do not seek care, are not tested, or are missed by reporting processes. Investigation and notification can proceed iteratively; this is a simplified sequence, not a universal operational timetable. Fallback: number the steps on paper. [CDC case surveillance](https://www.cdc.gov/nndss/what-is-case-surveillance/index.html).
:::

## Reportable and Notifiable Conditions

**Reportable:** Jurisdictional rules require reports to public health authorities. Lists and requirements vary.

**Nationally notifiable:** States voluntarily send qualifying case information to CDC for national monitoring.

The **National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System (NNDSS)** brings these notifications together.

::: {.notes}
Use during the preceding debrief. National notification is different from mandatory reporting within a jurisdiction. Standard case definitions support comparisons. Do not assume every national condition is reportable everywhere, or that every reported case meets criteria for national statistics. [CDC case surveillance](https://www.cdc.gov/nndss/what-is-case-surveillance/index.html).

A current example of change: general COVID-19 case notification ended in 2025; COVID-19-associated pediatric mortality became nationally notifiable in 2026. This does not mean that COVID-19 monitoring stopped. [CDC notice to data users](https://www.cdc.gov/nndss/infectious-disease/notice-to-data-users.html).
:::

## Exercise: An Early Warning

**Fictional scenario · Pairs · 5 minutes**

Emergency departments record an unusual increase in fever-and-cough visits this week. Laboratory results are still arriving.

1. What can we reasonably conclude now?
2. What information would help us interpret the signal?
3. What could explain the increase besides more infections?

Would waiting for death certificates answer the same question soon enough?

::: {.notes}
Allow 2 minutes to discuss and 3 to debrief using the next slide. We know recorded symptom-related visits increased, not that confirmed influenza incidence rose. Examine total visits, participating facilities, coding changes, laboratory results, and timing. Healthcare-seeking behavior or another respiratory infection could explain the signal. Timely investigation can begin before certainty. Death records describe a different outcome and are not a substitute for this early signal. Fallback: discuss the written scenario without a browser.
:::

## Syndromic Surveillance

Syndromic surveillance is **one form of public health surveillance**.

It uses timely information, such as symptoms recorded during emergency visits, to detect and monitor health threats.

CDC’s **National Syndromic Surveillance Program (NSSP)** helps combine and use these data.

An early signal can prompt investigation without establishing a diagnosis.

::: {.notes}
Use within the preceding debrief. Surveillance includes ongoing collection, analysis, interpretation, and sharing information for action. Syndromic surveillance can use information before and after diagnoses and monitor longer-term trends too. Its defining feature is not that it is the only timely form of surveillance. [CDC NSSP](https://www.cdc.gov/nssp/php/about/index.html).
:::

## Sources for Our Project Questions {.compact}

| Source | What it can offer |
|---|---|
| **NHIS** — National Health Interview Survey | Reported health conditions, functioning, and healthcare access |
| **NHANES** — National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey | Interviews, examinations, and laboratory measurements |
| **BRFSS** — Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System | State-level adult data on behaviors, chronic conditions, and preventive services |

The question determines which measurements and population we need.

::: {.notes}
Use 2 minutes of the next exercise's 10-minute allocation to introduce the sources. NHIS and NHANES are NCHS surveys. BRFSS is a CDC/state collaboration, not an NCHS survey. For any source, inspect eligible ages, sampling, years, exact items, geography, and survey weights before estimating prevalence. Sources: [NHIS](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhis/about/index.html), [NHANES](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/about/index.html), [BRFSS](https://www.cdc.gov/brfss/index.html).
:::

## Exercise: Which Source Fits?

**Project groups · 10 minutes with source table**

For our disease topic—or diabetes if we have not chosen one—complete:

“To learn **[what]** about **[whom]**, we would first examine **[source]** because **[reason]**. We would still need to check **[limitation]**.”

Name a measurement we need and a competing source that would answer a different question.

Our existing project still uses CDI or an approved alternative.

::: {.notes}
After 2 minutes with the source table, allow 3 minutes to formulate a question, 2 to examine the linked source description, and 3 to compare recommendations. Diabetes examples: NHIS for reported diagnosis and access; NHANES for measured markers that can identify previously undiagnosed disease; BRFSS for state comparisons of reported diagnosis or behaviors. Do not assume all sources support county estimates. The course project requirement is unchanged; this is a source-selection exercise. Fallback: use the preceding table on screen or paper; list documentation to check later.
:::

## Exercise: A Parkinson’s Registry Grows

**Hypothetical data—not TCU results · Pairs · 5 minutes**

A Parkinson’s registry adds two clinics and an online enrollment option. Enrollment rises from **200 to 350 people**.

Can we conclude that Parkinson’s incidence increased?

What would we need to know about diagnosis dates, duplicate records, and who could enroll?

Name one question this registry could help answer even without measuring population incidence.

::: {.notes}
Allow 2 minutes to discuss and 3 to debrief. Enrollment rose by 150 people, but newly enrolled people need not be newly diagnosed. Expanded recruitment alone could explain the increase. Population incidence requires new cases during a defined interval and an appropriate population at risk, with adequate case ascertainment. A registry can still help describe enrolled participants, support recruitment, or follow their outcomes. Do not generalize a clinic or volunteer registry to all residents. Fallback: write a conclusion and limitation on paper. This is a hypothetical design exercise, not a description of TCU's actual registry.
:::

## Exercise: Comparing Countries

**Fictional data · Pairs · 5 minutes**

Two countries each report **1,000 influenza cases** this month.

Country A reports laboratory-confirmed cases from selected hospitals. Country B reports symptom-defined cases from clinics nationwide.

Can we rank their influenza burden from these counts?

What would we need to make a useful comparison? What could international coordination contribute?

::: {.notes}
Allow 2 minutes for pairs and 3 for debrief with the next slide. Equal counts do not imply equal incidence. Definitions, testing, coverage, population denominators, and time periods must be considered. Simply dividing by each country's population does not resolve incompatible case definitions or coverage. Fallback: use the written scenario and collect one proposed improvement per pair.
:::

## International Coordination

WHO’s **Global Influenza Surveillance and Response System (GISRS)** connects national institutions that share respiratory-virus data.

Shared definitions and laboratory methods help us interpret differences between places.

International organizations can coordinate information; they cannot make missing or incompatible observations disappear.

::: {.notes}
Use within the preceding debrief. WHO coordinates collaboration among participating institutions; FluNet shares virologic surveillance data and FluID shares epidemiologic surveillance data. This connects local observations to global monitoring and response. [WHO GISRS](https://www.who.int/initiatives/global-influenza-surveillance-and-response-system).
:::

## Our Questions for Any Dataset

What question can these records answer?

Who and what do they count—and miss?

Does the denominator match the numerator?

What could change the records without changing disease occurrence?

::: {.notes}
Allow 1 minute to close. Invite students to carry these questions into their group projects. The preceding two checks take about 3 minutes together: individual choice, brief pair explanation, then debrief. Stop here for the core module; the following activity is optional.
:::

## Optional Exercise: Google Trends {.compact}

**Pairs · 9 minutes**

In [Google Trends](https://trends.google.com/trends/), compare the search terms **“elder abuse”** and **“elder mistreatment.”**

Use **United States · January 1–December 31, 2023 · Web Search**.

Write one sentence describing the search data and one tempting conclusion they cannot establish.

The **0–100 index** describes relative search interest, not numbers of people or cases. What else could make searches increase?

::: {.notes}
Allow 1 minute for setup, 3 to explore, 2 to write, and 3 to compare. Use search terms, not topics; record settings and do not require a specific peak. Relative interest is normalized within the comparison. News coverage, coursework, or changed terminology can alter searches; searching is not a validated disease count. Low-volume terms can appear as zero, and Google's statistical noise can produce misleading small spikes. [Google Trends explanation](https://support.google.com/trends/answer/4365533?hl=en).

Fallback: use simulated indices 25, 50, and 100 across three weeks, displayed on the next slide. Ask students to revise “Cases quadrupled.” The simulation illustrates interpretation, not real findings.
:::

## Google Trends: Offline Exercise

**Simulated relative search-interest indices**

| Week | Index |
|---|---:|
| 1 | 25 |
| 2 | 50 |
| 3 | 100 |

A headline says: “Cases quadrupled.”

What did the data actually measure? Write a better headline and give another possible explanation.

::: {.notes}
Use only if the preceding live activity is unavailable, within its 9-minute allocation. A defensible statement is that the simulated relative search-interest index increased from 25 to 100. These values do not count cases, people, or absolute searches. A public-awareness campaign could change the signal. Reinforce that association and prediction do not establish causation. Source for interpretation: [Google Trends explanation](https://support.google.com/trends/answer/4365533?hl=en).
:::
